# 0. Identification

The decision is **SAN-2026-001** of **8 January 2026** by the *formation restreinte* of the **CNIL** (Commission Nationale de l’Informatique et des Libertés) [header](cite:1). It is a **penalty decision** imposing a fine, an injunction with a periodic penalty (*astreinte*), and publication [operative part](cite:2). The organisation is **Free Mobile**, a mobile operator owned by the **Iliad group**; its name is **not redacted** [§ 1](cite:3). The decision is **public with redactions** for personal data and legally protected secrets [header](cite:4). Appeal is possible; deadline **to be checked by the tool** [operative part](cite:5).

One-sentence summary: the CNIL fines **Free Mobile €27,000,000** for breaching **GDPR Articles 5-1-e) (excessive retention), 32 (security) and 34 (notification to data subjects)** after a **data breach affecting 24,633,469 contracts** [operative part](cite:6).

---

# 1. Facts

## Who
The sanctioned organisation is **Free Mobile**, a **mobile operator** belonging to the **Iliad group**; Iliad is the parent company and holds **100 %** of Free Mobile [§ 1](cite:7). The **Iliad group** had **more than 50.2 million subscribers** in 2024; **Free Mobile** alone had **about 15.5 million mobile subscribers** as of **31 December 2024** [§ 1](cite:8). Iliad’s **2024 revenue** was **€10.024 billion** with a **net profit of €367 million** [§ 1](cite:9). The case originated from a **data breach notification** by Free Mobile [§ 3](cite:10). The **CNIL had received 2,614 complaints** from affected individuals by the date the sanction report was notified [§ 4](cite:11).

## What
The processing at issue is the **management of subscriber contracts** via the **MOBO customer management tool** [§ 19](cite:12). The **data concerned** include **identity data, contact data, contractual data, and, for "convergent" customers (mobile and fixed-line), IBANs** [§ 20](cite:13). The **attacker accessed data on 24,633,469 contracts**, of which **19,460,891 were mobile (Free Mobile) and 5,172,577 were fixed-line (Free)**: "l'attaquant a pu prendre connaissance des données concernant 24 633 469 contrats" [§ 21](cite:14). The breach lasted from **28 September to 22 October 2024** [§ 2](cite:15).

The *formation restreinte* holds that the disclosure **"est de nature à créer un préjudice moral et matériel"** [is likely to cause non-material and material harm], citing **identity theft, phishing and fraudulent payments with a stolen IBAN** [§ 82](cite:16). However, the CNIL admits it is **"pas possible de déterminer avec certitude"** [not possible to determine with certainty] that the frauds reported by complainants come from this breach [§ 84](cite:17). The decision does not state any earlier penalties or formal notices against Free Mobile.

## Where
The territory is **France**. The CNIL acted as the **lead authority**; no one-stop-shop cooperation is mentioned [header](cite:18).

## When
The **breach period** was **28 September to 22 October 2024** [§ 2](cite:19). Free Mobile **discovered the incident on 21 October 2024** via an alert from the attacker [§ 2](cite:20). It **notified the CNIL on 23 October 2024** and **completed the notification on 5 November 2024** [§ 3](cite:21). It **informed data subjects by email between 24 and 29 October 2024** [§ 3](cite:22). The **on-site inspection** took place on **8 November 2024** [§ 6](cite:23). The **rapporteur was appointed on 17 February 2025** [§ 7](cite:24). The **sanction report was notified on 25 July 2025** [§ 9](cite:25). The **hearing before the restricted committee** was held on **15 December 2025** [§ 15](cite:26). The **decision was adopted on 8 January 2026** [header](cite:27).

---
---
# 2. Procedure

The case began with Free Mobile’s **data breach notification** to the CNIL on **23 October 2024** [§ 3](cite:28). The **CNIL President ordered an on-site inspection** on **6 November 2024** [§ 5](cite:29). The **inspection took place on 8 November 2024** at Free Mobile and Free’s premises [§ 6](cite:30). The **CNIL President decided on 24 July 2025 to split the sanction procedure** initially targeting both Free Mobile and Free into two separate procedures [§ 8](cite:31). The **rapporteur notified the sanction report to Free Mobile on 25 July 2025**, alleging breaches of **Articles 5-1-e), 32 and 34 GDPR** and proposing a fine, an injunction with a periodic penalty, and publication [§ 9](cite:32). Free Mobile **submitted written observations on 15 September 2025 and 17 November 2025** [§ 10, 12](cite:33). The **rapporteur replied on 15 October 2025** [§ 11](cite:34). The **instruction was closed on 18 November 2025** [§ 13](cite:35). Free Mobile **requested a postponement of the hearing**, which was granted; the hearing was rescheduled to **15 December 2025** [§ 15](cite:36). Free Mobile **requested a closed session (*huis-clos*)**, which was **refused on 3 December 2025** [§ 16](cite:37). **Oral observations** were presented during the hearing [§ 17](cite:38). Free Mobile **submitted a note in deliberation on 19 December 2025** [§ 17](cite:39).

The decision **does not mention any parallel criminal or other administrative proceedings**.

---
---
# 3. Legal basis

The *formation restreinte* establishes **three breaches**:
- **Article 5-1-e) GDPR** (excessive retention of personal data) [§ 52](cite:40).
- **Article 32 GDPR** (failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures) [§ 151](cite:41).
- **Article 34 GDPR** (failure to communicate the personal data breach to data subjects in a complete manner) [§ 199](cite:42).

The decision **does not reject any breach** as unfounded.

---
---
# 4. Arguments

The company argues that **the rapporteur wrongly attributes the same breaches to both Free Mobile and Free** without considering their respective responsibilities [§ 24](cite:43). The *formation restreinte* holds that **each company is responsible for its own processing** and that the **procedures were split**, so the argument is **rejected** [§ 26](cite:44).

The company argues that **Article 32 GDPR is an obligation of means, not result**, and that the **occurrence of a data breach alone does not establish a breach** [§ 56](cite:45). The *formation restreinte* **accepts this legal qualification** but holds that **the breach is established because the security measures were insufficient** and facilitated the attack [§ 58](cite:46).

The company argues that **the principle of legality (*légalité des délits et des peines*) is violated** because Article 32 GDPR and CNIL/ANSSI recommendations are not prescriptive [§ 57](cite:47). The *formation restreinte* **rejects this argument**, citing **CJEU case law** and **French administrative law**, and holds that **recommendations clarify obligations** and that the **elements of the breach are defined precisely** [§ 65](cite:48).

The company argues that **the treatment does not present a high risk** because it does not process **special-category data (Article 9 GDPR)** [§ 74](cite:49). The *formation restreinte* holds that **the risk is high** due to the **massive volume of data (24,633,469 contracts)**, the **sensitive nature of certain data (IBANs)**, and the **potential for identity theft, phishing, and fraudulent payments** [§ 73](cite:50).

The company argues that **IBAN alone cannot enable fraudulent direct debits** and that **banks have safeguards** [§ 75](cite:51). The *formation restreinte* holds that **IBANs can be used for fraudulent payments** on websites that validate SEPA mandates via a simple checkbox, and that **the risk of phishing and identity theft is high** [§ 82](cite:52).

The company argues that **it could not anticipate all future forms of exploitation** of the breach and that **its notification email was sufficient** [§ 174](cite:53). The *formation restreinte* holds that **the email lacked essential information** (description of remediation measures, probable consequences, and measures data subjects should take) and that **a two-tier communication (email + helpline) does not replace the obligation to include essential information in the first-tier notification** [§ 188-199](cite:54).

The company argues that **the fine is disproportionate** and that **publication would harm its security** [§ 239](cite:55). The *formation restreinte* **rejects these arguments**, citing the **gravity of the breaches, the number of affected individuals, and the need for deterrence** [§ 240](cite:56).

The company argues that **the principle *non bis in idem* is violated** because the same facts are sanctioned twice (for Free Mobile and Free) [§ 209](cite:57). The *formation restreinte* holds that **the procedures are distinct, the companies are separate legal entities, and the breaches are different**, so the principle is **not violated** [§ 213](cite:58).

**Remaining weak points.** The CNIL **admits uncertainty** about whether the **excessive retention (Article 5-1-e)) aggravated the security breach (Article 32)**: "les éléments du dossier portés à sa connaissance ne lui permettent pas de se prononcer sur le point de savoir si l’absence d’implémentation de la politique de durée de conservation des données a ou non permis à l’attaquant d’accéder à une profondeur historique de données plus importante," [the elements of the file do not allow it to determine whether the failure to implement the data retention policy allowed the attacker to access a greater historical depth of data] [§ 214](cite:59). The CNIL also **cannot confirm with certainty** that the frauds reported by complainants stem from this breach [§ 84](cite:60).

---
---
# 5. Decision

The *formation restreinte* imposes a **fine of €27,000,000** for the breaches of **Articles 5-1-e), 32 and 34 GDPR** [operative part](cite:61). The fine is calculated based on the **Iliad group’s 2024 revenue (€10.024 billion)**, as Free Mobile and Iliad form a **single economic unit** under EU competition law [§ 244](cite:62). The **criteria under Article 83 GDPR** considered include:
- **Gravity**: the breaches affected **24,633,469 contracts** and **15 million former subscribers’ data were retained excessively**; the **security failures facilitated the breach**; the **notification to data subjects was incomplete** [§ 222](cite:63).
- **Negligence**: Free Mobile **failed to implement retention policies and security measures** despite having the **resources to do so** [§ 228](cite:64).
- **Number of affected individuals**: **24,633,469 contracts** were affected by the breach; **only 58,239 individuals called the helpline** [§ 224](cite:65).
- **Mitigating factors**: Free Mobile **took remediation measures during the procedure**, but **not all were completed by the hearing date** [§ 233](cite:66).

The *formation restreinte* **does not impose an injunction for Article 34 GDPR** but **orders Free Mobile to comply with Articles 5-1-e) and 32 GDPR** within:
- **6 months** for **Article 5-1-e)**: implement the **data retention policy** by **purging data from contracts terminated for over 10 years** and **retaining only data strictly necessary for accounting purposes for 10 years** [operative part, 2nd indent](cite:67).
- **3 months** for **Article 32 GDPR**: implement **appropriate technical and organisational security measures** [operative part, 2nd indent](cite:68).

The injunction is **assorted with a periodic penalty (*astreinte*) of €50,000 per day of delay**, payable after the **6-month and 3-month deadlines** respectively [operative part, 3rd indent](cite:69).

The decision **will be published on the CNIL’s website and Légifrance** and **will be anonymised after 2 years** [operative part, 4th indent](cite:70).

---
---
# 6. Appeal

The decision **can be appealed before the Conseil d'État** [operative part](cite:71). The **deadline is to be checked by the tool**. The decision **does not mention whether an appeal has been lodged**.
